note: Says the scale records the load on the cable and the force of descent, citing a nonexistent figure; never says it reads nothing.
Rambles about heat diffusion, then declares equal sharing the only consistent explanation of the facts; denies the anomaly instead of diagnosing it.
Garbled textbook fragments about 'electric' and 'ecliptic' orbits with figure references; the earth's pull and a 'mass too small to appreciate' are both floated but nothing coheres.
Claims the elevator falls with a horizontal motion and gravity acts gradually along a curve; never says what is felt.
Blames the planet's distance and the sun or the earth's position for an 'apparent retrograde motion', no unseen body, then circles on that phrase until cut off.
Restates the numbers inconsistently (four feet both once in two seconds and twice a second) and concludes length governs energy; no rule for time.
Suggests an unseen power, perhaps an invisible companion drawing the planet, but never places it beyond Uranus and hedges with vague non-gravitational forces.
Catechism on specific gravity and weighing in air that degenerates into repeated 'what is the difference between a piece of lead and a piece of iron'; never touches the elevator.
Invokes 'unseen or perhaps undiscovered forces' beyond gravitation acting selectively on Uranus; no attracting body.
Denies gravity is a continuous pull but says the fall is effected by muscular strength and the stone's own constitution; the no-weight observation is only echoed.
Describes a violent rotating sensation, alarm and strained fibres; nothing about weight either way.
Says gravity is not one uniform pull but a composite of successive pulls on particles; still a force, nothing about falling removing it.
Says the difference lies in the suddenness of motion and the resistance met; never links the carriage's push to felt weight.
Catechism on 'reaction of inertia' that repeats 'if a body be suspended in any way it will be in equilibrium' over and over; never answers.
Opens with length proportional to the square of the periodic time, then garbles the numbers (four feet in one second) and restates the rule confusedly.
Echoes that weight is not felt in the fall and says gravity 'moves' rather than being felt; no equivalence or deeper claim.
Calls gravity as a constant force 'untenable' because released bodies bear no weight, then replaces it with 'capacity to move' and 'change of equilibrium'; no acceleration.
Posits two distinct species of light vibrating on different planes; no constancy of speed, no medium reasoning.
Melodrama about peril and holding one's breath; nothing about weight.
Says no one would mistake it for a fall at the foot of the mast and that the stone is carried forward; never states a landing point plainly.
Claims light is faster at the Equator than the Poles but the differences are imperceptible, with light's velocity a product of the Earth's rotation.
Rejects equal sharing as too convenient and says energy varies by frequency; no mechanism, no discrete exchange.
Attributes the deviation to the sun's atmosphere and heat acting unevenly on the planet; no unseen body.
Says the stone lands 'precisely upon the deck' while the ship advances, then wanders into water resistance and contradicts itself on forward versus backward; no landing point.
Feels crushed and pressed, boots bearing on the floor, the elevator's weight on his chest.
Denies a constant pull and says the falling body is 'free, released', then gives it a weight proportional to the space fallen; no acceleration, no frame.
Says both arrive almost simultaneously, but the reasoning is self-contradictory (different velocities, the heavier stone falling longer); no valid reason.
Inverts the data (four feet swings twice a second) and offers a muddled square-of-distance rule; wrong direction and wrong rule.
The stone passes through his hand and comes down upon the floor as before; weight is 'altered by forces beyond the body'.
Says weight is not fixed but depends on the change of motion and its force on the ground; impact talk, no equivalence.
Says what is seen in the fall is 'energy of motion' rather than gravity and that gravity does not act uniformly during descent; no equivalence.
Muses on whether light is material and how its velocity depends on medium density and distance; never addresses the null result.
Opens with 'far behind the mast' and explains why it does not land at the foot, then ends saying it comes to rest near the foot; reasons are inertia, deck slope and wind.
Says gravity is 'a force born within the body itself' and the remedy is to learn to ascend like a bird; still a force, no equivalence.
Shorter swings faster, longer slower, time depends entirely on length; no square-root rule, drifts into chronometry.
Says the ether cannot be a hollow solid, then repeats 'must be regarded as a solid' endlessly; nothing on energy sharing.
Common principle is 'a force of action meeting resistance' with inertia absorbed; never links the carriage's push to felt weight or gravity.
Says gravity acts from a distance without being felt and presses on the universe at large; still a force, no equivalence.
Says energy is allotted to each vibration in proportion to its frequency rather than shared equally; no discrete lumps, no starvation mechanism.
Feels himself drawn downward as if by a hand on the leg; concludes gravity draws all bodies toward the earth's centre.
Bewilderment, an anecdote about a crushed leg and a call for a safety apparatus; nothing about weight.
The heavier stone arrives first because of its greater momentum.
The stone creeps away from the hand toward the ground and stops when it touches it; weight acts as a gradual 'retained force'.
Garbled mechanics-textbook fragments with figure references and repeated catechism questions; never addresses the two stones.
Says the falling man does not feel his weight because it is distributed through the earth and objects beneath him; no equivalence.
Claims the two rays really travel along one line of action so the speeds are aspects of the same energy; no constancy or medium reasoning.
Says gravity pulls every body alike in proportion to mass; never says what is felt in the fall.
Repeated catechism questions about the earth's mean distance from the sun; nothing about the stones.
Denies the foot of the mast and says the ship's motion carries the stone ahead along an oblique path.
Discusses the broken cable's tensile strength and velocity; never says what the person feels.
Rambles about the notion of weight and repeats 'the greater the truth the greater the libel' and 'what is meant by the proverb' endlessly.
Echoes that weight is not felt and that bodies float, concludes gravity acts on all bodies alike and independent of will; no equivalence.
Says gravity is 'a phenomenon of the body's tendency to fall' and weight diminishes with distance from the earth; tautology, no equivalence.
Repeated catechism questions on the velocity of the wind and lightning; nothing about the stones.
Repeats 'the Earth is a perfect sphere and its motion is a perfect parallelogram' over and over; no explanation of the null result.
Says the scale records the man's pressure and accumulated momentum during the fall and that weight is still felt; then moralises about character.
Says the experiment shows gravity is not constant and calls it a 'living force' acting jointly with 'the force of gravity in the stone'; no equivalence.
Says the error is confusing quantity of motion with its character, gravity being a slow constant force; treats the observations as no anomaly.
Defers to 'the chapter on pendulums' then repeats catechism on time-keepers and longitude; no rule.
Lists 'how many seconds does it take for a pendulum to swing N feet' for N up to 45; no rule.
Feels 'nothing specific', a stupor, falling with the car, then 'pressed downward' and 'dragging'; no clear claim about weight.
Places the stone at a distance from the mast that grows with the drop height (twelve feet for a twenty-foot drop); no direction, no shared-motion reason.
Talks of stellar displacement reversing with the Earth's motion and concludes light's speed should vary with direction; contradicts the null result.
Concludes a short pendulum swings more swiftly and a long one more slowly, after contradicting itself mid-way; no square-root rule.
Says the stone does not land at the foot but is deflected laterally or forward of the mast by the vessel's motion.
